input: whats the pair of cpu registers that lets each program act like it starts at address 0?
expected_output: It is the base and bounds pair: a base register and a bounds register (sometimes called a limit register), kept in each CPU. Together they let the OS place the address space anywhere in physical memory while ensuring the process can only access its own address space.

evidence.quote: Specifically, we’ll need two hardware registers within each CPU: one is called the base register, and the other the bounds (sometimes called a limit register).
This base-and-bounds pair is going to allow us to place the address space anywhere we’d like in physical memory, and do so while ensuring that the process can only access its own address space.

input: What does it mean for the hardware to translate addresses on every memory reference, and what does the OS still have to do?
expected_output: The hardware changes the virtual address an instruction uses (for a fetch, load, or store) into the physical address where the data actually lives. The hardware only provides the low-level mechanism, so the OS must set it up so the right translations happen, and manage memory by tracking which locations are free and which are in use.

evidence.quote: With address translation, the hardware transforms each memory access (e.g., an instruction fetch, load, or store), changing the virtual address provided by the instruction to a physical address where the desired information is actually located.
The OS must get involved at key points to set up the hardware so that the correct translations take place; it must thus manage memory, keeping track of which locations are free and which are in use

input: if the base register already shifts every address to the right spot, why bother with a second register at all?
expected_output: The second register, the bounds (limit) register, is there for protection. The processor first checks that the memory reference is within bounds so it is legal, and if a process generates an address greater than the bounds or a negative one, the CPU raises an exception and the process will likely be terminated.

evidence.quote: the bounds register is there to help with protection. Specifically, the processor will first check that the memory reference is within bounds to make sure it is legal;
If a process generates a virtual address that is greater than the bounds, or one that is negative, the CPU will raise an exception, and the process will likely be terminated.

input: why does the os save and restore base and bounds on every context switch?
expected_output: Each CPU has only one base and bounds register pair, and their values differ for each running program because each is loaded at a different physical address. So when the OS stops a process it saves the two values to memory in a per-process structure such as the PCB, and when it resumes the process it sets them back to that process's values.

evidence.quote: There is only one base and bounds register pair on each CPU, after all, and their values differ for each running program, as each program is loaded at a different physical address in memory.

when the OS decides to stop running a process, it must save the values of the base and bounds registers to memory, in some per-process structure such as the process structure or process control block (PCB).
Similarly, when the OS resumes a running process (or runs it the first time), it must set the values of the base and bounds on the CPU to the correct values for this process.

input: how can the os move a stopped process to a different part of ram without it noticing?
expected_output: The OS first deschedules the process, copies its address space from the current location to the new one, and then updates the saved base register in the process structure to point to the new location. When the process is resumed, the new base register is restored and it runs again, oblivious that its instructions and data are in a completely new spot in memory.

evidence.quote: To move a process’s address space, the OS first deschedules the process; then, the OS copies the address space from the current location to the new location; finally, the OS updates the saved base register (in the process structure) to point to the new location.
When the process is resumed, its (new) base register is restored, and it begins running again, oblivious that its instructions and data are now in a completely new spot in memory.

input: what stops a normal app from just rewriting the relocation offset so it points into some other process's memory?
expected_output: The instructions that modify the base and bounds registers are privileged, so they can only be run in kernel (privileged) mode. If a user program tries to change those registers, the CPU raises an exception and runs the OS handler for trying to execute a privileged operation while in user mode.

evidence.quote: These instructions are privileged; only in kernel (or privileged) mode can the registers be modified.

Similarly, if a user program tries to change the values of the (privileged) base and bounds registers, the CPU should raise an exception and run the “tried to execute a privileged operation while in user mode” handler.

input: In the little x86 example that bumps a variable by three, what does each of the three instructions do, and how does the code know where the variable lives?
expected_output: It presumes the address of the variable has already been placed in the register ebx. The first movl instruction loads the value at that address into the general-purpose register eax, the addl instruction adds 3 to eax, and the final movl stores the value in eax back into memory at that same location.

evidence.quote: it presumes that the address of x has been placed in the register ebx, and then loads the value at that address into the general-purpose register eax using the movl instruction (for “longword” move). The next instruction adds 3 to eax, and the final instruction stores the value in eax back into memory at that same location.

input: How did the old purely-software way of relocating a program work, and what made the hardware approach better?
expected_output: In the software approach (static relocation), a piece of software called the loader takes an executable about to be run and rewrites its addresses to the desired offset in physical memory. Its biggest problem is that it does not provide protection, since processes can generate bad addresses and illegally access other processes' or even OS memory; another negative is that once placed, an address space is difficult to relocate later. The hardware approach (base and bounds) fixes both: a bounds register ensures addresses stay within the address space, giving the protection that generally needs hardware support, and because translation happens at runtime, address spaces can be moved even after the process has started running.

evidence.quote: The basic technique is referred to as static relocation, in which a piece of software known as the loader takes an executable that is about to be run and rewrites its addresses to the desired offset in physical memory.
First and most importantly, it does not provide protection, as processes can generate bad addresses and thus illegally access other process’s or even OS memory;
Because this relocation of the address happens at runtime, and because we can move address spaces even after the process has started running, the technique is often referred to as dynamic relocation
Another negative is that once placed, it is difficult to later relocate an address space to another location
in general, hardware support is likely needed for true protection
A bounds (or limit) register ensures that such addresses are within the confines of the address space.

input: is the limit register a size or an end address, and does it change the check?
expected_output: There are two ways to define it. If it holds the size of the address space, the hardware checks the virtual address against it first and then adds the base. If it holds the physical address of the end of the address space, the hardware first adds the base and then checks that the result is within bounds. Both are logically equivalent.

evidence.quote: In one way (as above), it holds the size of the address space, and thus the hardware checks the virtual address against it first before adding the base.
In the second way, it holds the physical address of the end of the address space, and thus the hardware first adds the base and then makes sure the address is within bounds.
Both methods are logically equivalent; for simplicity, we’ll usually assume the former method.

input: address space is 8 KB, loaded at physical 40 KB. what physical address is virtual 2000, and what about virtual 9000?
expected_output: The hardware adds the base register to the virtual address. The base is 40 KB = 40960, so virtual 2000 becomes 40960 + 2000 = 42960. Virtual 9000 is bigger than the 8 KB (8192-byte) address space, so it is too big and the result is a fault that raises an exception.

evidence.quote: Each memory reference generated by the process is a virtual address; the hardware in turn adds the contents of the base register to this address and the result is a physical address that can be issued to the memory system.
Only if the virtual address is “too big” or negative will the result be a fault, causing an exception to be raised.
Specifically, the processor will first check that the memory reference is within bounds to make sure it is legal; in the simple example above, the bounds register would always be set to 16 KB.

input: 64 KB in four 16 KB slots: os in 1st, A 2nd, B 4th. whats on the free list after C starts and A exits?
expected_output: The free list is a list of ranges of physical memory not currently in use. When C is created, the OS searches the free list to find room for its address space and marks it used, so the only free slot (32 KB-48 KB) goes to C and the list is empty. When A exits, the OS puts A's memory (16 KB-32 KB) back on the free list, so that slot is all that is on it.

evidence.quote: a free list, which simply is a list of the ranges of the physical memory which are not currently in use.
When a new process is created, the OS will have to search a data structure (often called a free list) to find room for the new address space and then mark it used.
Upon termination of a process, the OS thus puts its memory back on the free list, and cleans up any associated data structures as need be.

input: so the compiler must pick the real ram addresses a program will sit at, and bake them into the binary, right?
expected_output: No. With base and bounds, each program is written and compiled as if it is loaded at address zero. When the program starts running, the OS decides where in physical memory to load it and sets the base register to that value. The process has no idea its memory references are being translated.

input: if my program reads some address way outside what it owns, does the entire computer die or what
expected_output: No. The CPU stops executing the user program and arranges for the OS's out-of-bounds exception handler to run. The handler figures out how to react, most likely terminating the offending process, since the OS is protective of the machine.

evidence.quote: the CPU should stop executing the user program and arrange for the OS “out-of-bounds” exception handler to run. The OS handler can then figure out how to react, in this case likely terminating the process.
The common reaction of the OS will be one of hostility: it will likely terminate the offending process.
The OS should be highly protective of the machine it is running, and thus it does not take kindly to a process trying to access memory or execute instructions that it shouldn’t.

input: why do only a few programs fit in ram when each wastes part of its fixed slot?
expected_output: Each relocated process sits in a fixed-sized slot, and because its stack and heap are not big, the space between them is simply wasted. This waste inside the allocated unit is called internal fragmentation, and it can limit how many processes fit even if there is enough physical memory.

evidence.quote: In our current approach, although there might be enough physical memory for more processes, we are currently restricted to placing an address space in a fixed-sized slot and thus internal fragmentation can arise
however, because the process stack and heap are not too big, all of the space between the two is simply wasted.
This type of waste is usually called internal fragmentation, as the space inside the allocated unit is not all used (i.e., is fragmented) and thus wasted.
